analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans offshore oil and gas drilling off Washington, Oregon, and California.
analysis.headline: The bill to permanently ban offshore oil and gas leasing off the Washington, Oregon, and Northern and Central California coasts died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to bar the Interior Department from ever issuing a lease for oil or gas exploration, development, or production in three federal offshore planning areas off Washington, Oregon, and Northern and Central California [S2] [S3]. Because it writes the ban into law rather than relying on a presidential order, it would protect those waters even if a future administration wanted to open them to drilling [S3]. It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, then to its energy subcommittee, and never advanced to a floor vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, fishing and shellfish industries, tourism businesses, and everyone who uses the Pacific coast would gain protection from oil spills and the industrial infrastructure that comes with offshore drilling. Because the ban would be written into statute, it would also guard against a future administration reversing a presidential drilling withdrawal. Americans broadly would get a modest climate benefit from keeping those reserves unburned [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal communities, fisheries, and beach tourism

how_it_helps.text: Permanently prohibits Interior from leasing the Washington/Oregon, Northern California, and Central Pacific planning areas for oil and gas exploration, development, or production, protecting those waters from spills and drilling infrastructure no matter which party controls the White House
Writes the ban into the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act itself, making it much harder to undo than a presidential memorandum, which a later president can revoke

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose access to potential offshore reserves in those three planning areas. To a lesser degree, the public forgoes whatever royalties, jobs, and domestic production those areas might have generated, and energy markets lose a potential future supply source [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies seeking new reserves

drawbacks.text: A permanent ban forgoes any future domestic oil and gas production, jobs, and federal royalty revenue from those offshore areas, and shrinking potential supply can put modest upward pressure on energy prices

The bill addresses only drilling in these three planning areas; it does nothing about existing fossil fuel production elsewhere, so its climate and coastal benefits, while real, are regional rather than economy-wide
The ban is legally permanent even if an emergency energy shortage someday made tapping those reserves attractive, with no escape clause

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is durable protection of a long, heavily used coastline from oil spills and drilling infrastructure, locked in by statute against future political reversals. The cost falls mainly on one industry that currently has no active leases in those waters, plus forgone potential royalties and supply. On balance the benefits are broad and the costs concentrated and speculative, though the permanence of the ban means the tradeoff can never be revisited by a future Congress choosing differently.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and its energy subcommittee for the rest of the two-year session and was never voted on by the full House.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Huffman introduced the bill on May 7, 2021, and it was immediately referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources
Five days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, which held a hearing but took no further action

Twenty-six House Democrats cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats and none from outside the West Coast delegation's allies, but the committee never voted to send it to the floor before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies remain legally able to seek leases in those waters, and opponents of drilling are left relying on presidential withdrawal orders that a future president could reverse.

for.name: Rep. Jared Huffman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently ban oil and gas leasing off the Washington, Oregon, and Northern and Central California coasts

for.name: 26 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans signed on

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, referred it to its energy subcommittee, held one hearing, and never voted it out of committee or scheduled it for the floor before the Congress ended

against.name: Offshore oil and gas industry
against.role: Would-be lessees of the protected waters
against.what_they_did: Had a direct financial interest in keeping the planning areas open to leasing; the bill's passage would have permanently closed them

sides.party_line_note: All 26 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, but the bill never reached a floor vote where party splits would have been recorded.

industries.note: The bill permanently closes three federal planning areas off the West Coast to new oil and gas leases, eliminating any future production, revenue, or jobs the industry might have drawn from them. Their interest in keeping the areas open runs directly against the coastal protection and climate benefits the bill's supporters sought.

A permanent drilling ban protects the fisheries, beaches, and coastal economies of Washington, Oregon, and California from spill risk and offshore infrastructure. The industry's interest here runs alongside the public's.
